notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0057.tlg075.1st1K-gr: 'If the person was fastidious' renders εἰ καθαρότητος ἄνθρωπος εἴη, literally 'if the person were of cleanliness'; the phrase is odd and may be corrupt.

'Flavours' renders *chymoi*, which can also mean humours; the reference back to Book 4 on qualities of taste shows flavours are meant. *Antiphrazontes*: apparently books giving cover-names for drugs; the exact sense of the title is uncertain. Tanitros: not identified, and the name may be corrupt; 'the [follower] of Asclepiades' could also be 'the [work] of Asclepiades'. 'Horoscopes' (*hōroskopoi*) are the thirty-six decans, the star-groups that mark the rising hours. *Ophionika* of Konchlas: title not otherwise known; Galen says the author is fictitious. *agrōstis*: a grass, perhaps couch grass or Bermuda grass. The text's Ἀριχιγένην and Διοσκουρδίου are taken as slips for Archigenes and Dioscorides.

Ateuristus is unidentified; the name may be corrupt. In the chilblains sentence ὑπερεχούσας does not construe; translated as if a verb of smearing stood there. ‘Play the Phoenician’ and ‘play the Lesbian’ (φοινικίζοντας, λεσβιαζόντων) are Greek slang for cunnilingus and fellatio respectively; κίναιδος is rendered ‘catamite’. ‘τὰ μέν γε πλεῖστα εἶναι τούτων ἐστὶ’ is garbled, though the sense is clear. ‘In it [this book]’: αὐτῷ may refer to this book or loosely to the treatise.

nodes.text: Preface. Having undertaken to write on the character and power of simple drugs, in the first two books we chose to expose the faulty methods of argument by which most of the more recent physicians go very greatly astray. In the third we made a kind of elementary introduction to the whole teaching; then next, in the fourth, we inquired into the nature of flavours, striving to discover everything that it is possible to gain from them towards the knowledge of the powers. At the end of that book we also discussed the qualities in simple drugs that relate to smell. In the fifth, passing on to the remaining class of powers, which takes its name from the effects they naturally produce, there too we demonstrated the nature and substance of each. All the general accounts of the power of simples, then, seem now to be complete; it is time to move on to the particular ones, or those by species, or however one may wish to name them. These would be worked out for each drug separately, as we also did right at the start, examining water and vinegar in the first of these treatises and oil and rose oil in the second; except that there our discussion proceeded by way of examples, against those who had pronounced incorrectly about their power, whereas here I shall go through each briefly, no longer concerned whether anyone has pronounced badly about any of them, but writing what seems to me most true, without controversy against those who are mistaken. That the account will not only be unclear to those who forget what came before, but will also lack the credibility of demonstration, is clear, I think, even if I do not say it; but it is perhaps better that I too should remind [the reader], first, that the test of the power of drugs must be made on the best-tempered constitution, and next, on simple diseases. And if anyone should wish to draw inferences by way of indication about the power itself from the qualities of taste as well, we showed the method for these too in the fourth [book]. So if anyone, having read the earlier books carelessly, or not having read them at all, comes straight to this book, in a hurry to gain knowledge of the power of drugs as quickly as possible, he will not have a secure knowledge of them. Since of all drugs some are parts of animals or plants or fruits, or certain saps or juices of these, while others are taken from mines, it seemed better to me to go through plants first, because their class is both the largest and the strongest in power, then next to speak of the mined substances, and then in this way to come to the parts of animals. And indeed I decided that the order of writing about them should also be made by letters, writing first about those plants whose names begin with the letter alpha, second those that begin with beta, and so on to the third, fourth, fifth and all the rest in succession according to the order of the letters. This is how Pamphilus too composed his treatise on herbs. But he turned aside into certain old wives' tales and some silly Egyptian sorceries, together with certain incantations which people pronounce over the herbs as they gather them. And indeed he has used [them] for amulets and other trickeries which are not only idle curiosities, nor merely outside the art of medicine, but are also all false. We, however, shall mention none of these things, nor, further, their silly metamorphoses. For we do not suppose such tales to be useful even to very small children, let alone to those eager to pursue the works of medicine. And it seems to me that 'life is short, the art long' was said by Hippocrates right at the beginning of the Aphorisms so that we should not use up our time on useless things, but should hasten, as far as we can, to take the shortest route through the most useful parts of the art themselves. Moreover, it seemed to me superfluous to add here these many Egyptian and Babylonian names of the herbs, and all those that some people have given them privately or symbolically. For it is better, if anyone wishes to busy himself with these too, to read on his own and by himself the books of synonyms [lists of alternative names]. For that is how those who compile them title them, as Xenocrates of Aphrodisias also did, a man in other respects much given to curious lore and not free of sorcery. As for Pamphilus, who composed the work on herbs, it is plain from what he writes himself that he is a grammarian who has neither seen the herbs he describes nor tested their power, but has trusted all who wrote before him without scrutiny. He copied out books, pointlessly adding a mass of names for each herb, then next relating whether any of them had been transformed from a human being, then adding incantations and certain libations and fumigations for taking them up out of the earth, and other silly sorceries of that kind. But Dioscorides of Anazarbus wrote in five books on the material useful for everything, recording not only herbs but also trees, fruits, juices and saps, and further all the mined substances and the parts of animals. And he seems to me to have produced the most complete treatise of all on the material of drugs. For much was well written about them by earlier writers too, but by no one in this way about all of them, unless one were to praise Tanitros, the [follower] of Asclepiades; for by him too other things are said well, except for his reasonings about causes. Whoever wishes to become experienced in materia medica should read these, and in addition the works of Heraclides of Tarentum, Crateuas and Mantias. But these men did not write in the same way, nor is everything gathered into one, as with Dioscorides, who titled his five books *On Material*; rather they wrote separately, as it happened, on the preparation and testing of drugs, as Heraclides of Tarentum did, and separately on purgation, or preliminary draughts, or clysters, as Mantias did; and separately on easily obtained remedies, like Apollonius, or on remedies by [bodily] region, like Mantias. Most of the use of drugs, however, has been written up in the therapeutic treatises themselves, both by the ancients and also by nearly all the more recent writers; for much was said by Hippocrates, and by Euryphon, Dieuches, Diocles, Pleistonicus, Praxagoras and Herophilus, and there is no ancient man who did not contribute something to the art, more or less, towards the knowledge of drugs, without the sorcery and imposture that Andreas later displayed; so that whoever has leisure to spend time with useful books written about drugs has many from the ancients, as has been said, and not a few from the more recent writers, down to the circle of Pamphilus and Archigenes. Moreover, Rufus of Ephesus also wrote of many drugs in his therapeutic books, and four [books] on herbs in hexameter verse were composed by him; and there is no fear of useful books running out, even if someone wishes to read nothing else all his life but [books] about drugs. One should, however, keep away from Andreas and those who are similar impostors, and much more still from Pamphilus, who has never seen, even in a dream, the herbs whose forms he attempts to describe. For people of this kind, as indeed Heraclides of Tarentum likened them, are most like the criers who announce the marks of appearance of a runaway slave without ever having seen him themselves. For they get the marks from those who know, and recite them like an incantation, though they could not recognise them even if the man being cried happened to be standing beside them. For my part, I used to find fault with those who first wrote descriptions of the forms of herbs, thinking it better for the learner to become an eyewitness at the side of the teacher himself, and not to become like the helmsmen [who learn] from a book. For in this way the teaching would be carried out more truly and more clearly by teachers, not of herbs only, or shrubs or trees, but of all other drugs as well. But if one does after all need a book, who is so wretched as to pass over those of Dioscorides, Niger, Heraclides, Crateuas and countless others who grew old in the art, and put up with the grammarian's books of a man writing incantations and metamorphoses and the sacred herbs of decans and demons? That sorcerers, men who have made it their business to astound the great crowd, put such things together, you can learn from the books of Pamphilus themselves, who first wrote up among the herbs southernwood, which happens to be familiar to all of us, then next the chaste tree, this too a quite familiar shrub, then *agrōstis* [couch grass], a plant not unknown even to laymen, then alkanet, of which no one is ignorant either, as indeed no one is of maidenhair, written next after it. In these, then, he writes nothing beyond what we know; but after these he mentions a herb called, as he says himself, 'eagle', about which he admits that none of the Greeks has said anything, but that it is written in one of the books attributed to Hermes the Egyptian, which contains the thirty-six sacred herbs of the horoscopes; these are all plainly nonsense and fictions of the compiler, very like the *Ophionika* ['Snake-Victories'] of Konchlas. For there never was any Konchlas at all; the name was put together as a joke, as was everything else written in his book. And these thirty-six herbs go no further than their names, with no real thing underlying them. But Pamphilus, like many others, perhaps had leisure to write useless tales into books; we, even now, consider that we are wasting our time by mentioning them any further. Let us begin, then, at once on the useful things.

[10. On *glykysidē*.] *Glykysidē* [peony], which people also call *pentorobos* and *paionia*, has a root that is gently astringent with a certain sweetness, and, when chewed for longer, also a somewhat bitter sharpness. For this reason it moves the menses when drunk with honey-water in the amount of an almond; one must, of course, pound it and sift it and sprinkle it in that way. It also clears out an obstructed liver, and the kidneys. But these effects it naturally produces insofar as it is sharp and somewhat bitter; insofar as it also has something astringent, it stops fluxes of the belly. In that case one should boil it down in one of the harsh wines and drink it. On the whole it is strongly drying in its power, so that I would not rule out that it has with good reason been believed to cure the epilepsy of young children even when hung on [them] as an amulet. And indeed I once knew a child who for eight months was not seized at all from the time he wore some of the root; but when the amulet somehow slipped off his neck, he was seized at once, and when another was hung on him again he was once more perfectly well. It seemed better to me to remove it yet again for the sake of a test; and when we had done so and he was convulsed once more, we hung a large, fresh piece of the root from his neck, and from then on the boy became completely healthy for the rest of the time and was never seized again. It was reasonable, then, [to suppose] either that certain particles flowing off the root, and then drawn in through breathing, treat the affected places in this way, or else that the air itself is turned and altered by the root. For in this way too the Cyrenaic sap [silphium] benefits an inflamed uvula, and roasted nigella visibly dries up catarrhs and head-colds, if one ties it up hot in a loosely woven linen cloth and continually draws in the heat from it by breathing through the nostrils. Moreover, if you put several threads, especially [ones dyed] with sea-purple, around a viper's neck and strangle the viper with them, and then tie each of the threads round the neck [of a patient], it is wonderfully beneficial for swollen tonsils and for whatever breaks out about the neck. But about such things I may perhaps go through them separately some time. As for the temperament of peony, one must understand that it is fine-particled and drying, yet not noticeably hot, but either balanced or slightly hotter.

None of what is now going to be said will be of much benefit to those who do not know what was said at the outset of this treatise, in the first five books; and some of it may perhaps even harm anyone who uses the drugs written about in it [this book] without having a method. I shall therefore speak to you as one who has learned those things, after reminding you of the main point of the whole treatise. It was shown that drugs, by the so-called active qualities, exert heat and cold and dryness and moisture, and that through the mixture of these they become astringent and harsh, salty and briny, bitter, pungent and sweet; and that some are cleansing, others repelling, others drawing, others softening, others burning, others putrefying, others crust-forming; and besides these, further, according to other more specific actions, flesh-forming and scar-forming and gluing together fistulas or wounds, or reducing overgrown flesh. It was also shown that the general power is discovered by way of indication from a single trial, and not just any chance trial, but one made with the distinctions that were stated; and that once the general power has been discovered, there is no longer any need of trial for the particular actions, except only to confirm what reason has found. Let us, then, now too make our assessment of the material before us in this way; and this is the material from animals. For in the three books following the fifth, the sixth, seventh and eighth, we went through the material from plants: not, obviously, all of it throughout the whole inhabited world, but as much as we have experience of; and in the book before this one, the ninth of the whole treatise, the material from earthy and stony bodies. It still remains for us to deal with the material from animals; and after that there is still left [the material] of things produced in the sea and in lakes, or in water generally, which are neither plants nor earth nor stone nor animal. Such things are very few altogether, and they will be written about last, after we have gone through what concerns the bodies of animals. The order of instruction for these too will follow the order of the first letters of their names. And just as, with the material from plants, I also gave an account of the juices that come from them, so now too the instruction about power will cover not only the solid parts in animals but also what is contained in them: phlegm, bile, blood, urine, dung and the like. Now in what was said earlier, not many of the individual items in the materials recorded by physicians remained unknown to me; I was eager to learn their powers myself through trial, and if there was any I did not know, I did not write about it at all, not thinking it right to trust others even about a single such thing, because I had found that some tell many lies. With the material now before us, it is not so. I admit that there are a great many of the parts, and of the fluids contained in the bodies of animals, of which I myself have had no trial of the kind that some have written about. For some of them are indecent and disgusting, and some are even forbidden by the laws. About these I do not know how Xenocrates came to write, a man who lived not long ago but in our grandfathers’ time, when Roman rule had forbidden the eating of human beings; but he at any rate, as though he had tried them himself, writes quite convincingly what conditions a human brain naturally cures when eaten, or human flesh or liver; and what the bones of the head or shin or fingers [cure] when drunk, some burnt and some unburnt; and what the blood itself [cures]. These things, then, even if against the laws, are at least not indecent. But the drinking of sweat and urine and a woman’s menstrual blood is indecent and disgusting, and no less so than these is dung, about which Xenocrates wrote what in the world it can do when smeared on the parts of the mouth and throat and when swallowed into the stomach; he has also written about ear-wax when swallowed. I for my part would not have brought myself to swallow even that, even on condition of never falling ill. And I consider dung far more disgusting than it. Indeed, it is a greater reproach for a decent man to be called a dung-eater than a doer of obscenities or a catamite; and even among those who do obscenities, we loathe those who ‘play the Phoenician’ more than those who ‘play the Lesbian’; and the man who drinks menstrual blood seems to me to undergo something close to that. So no man in his natural senses would bring himself to make trial of these things, nor of those that are more moderate than these but still indecent: having some part of the body smeared with dung for the sake of a condition in it, or with human semen. Xenocrates is accustomed to call this *gonos* [seed], and he distinguishes with all care which [conditions] the seed alone by itself naturally benefits when smeared on, and which [it benefits] after the intercourse of a man and a woman, when it has fallen out of the woman’s passage. There would have to be a great dearth of remedies for anyone to treat chilblains with a man’s semen that has not stayed inside but has flowed out of the woman after intercourse. There is a great deal of this kind of material too in what he wrote on the benefit [to be had] from animals. For he describes not only, of course, what power human urine has when drunk, or dung when swallowed and smeared on the parts in the mouth, but also [that] of each of the other animals, and much else that is hard to obtain, as when he mentions [the parts] of an elephant or a hippopotamus. The basilisk, that beast, I have never even seen; and if what is said about it is true, it is dangerous even to come near this animal. Certain others too have written about animals much as Xenocrates did, and Xenocrates himself copied most of his material from them. For how could he himself have had the means to make trial of so many things of such a kind? Attalus, for instance, who was once our king, evidently writes of fewer, although he applied himself most ambitiously to testing such things. And someone who praised Ateuristus’ treatise on the same subject gave it to me as well to go through; it was, as it seems to me at least, composed without any first-hand observation by its writer. I, then, will mention neither basilisks nor elephants nor hippopotamuses, nor anything else of which I have no experience myself; and the so-called love-potions, attraction spells, dream-senders and hate-charms (for I use their very names on purpose) I would not have mentioned in writing at all, not even if I had had sufficient experience of them, just as [I would not mention] deadly drugs either, or those which they themselves call ‘affliction-makers’. For some of their claims are actually ridiculous: binding one’s opponents in a lawsuit so that they cannot utter a word in court, or making a pregnant woman miscarry, or never conceive, and all the other things of that kind. Most of these are, by the evidence of trial as well, impossible; and some, even if possible, are at any rate harmful to human life, so that I wonder, by the gods, with what intention some people came to write them down. For things that bring disgrace even on the living once they are known, how did they hope that these would bring them good repute after death? Now if they were kings and made trial of them on men condemned to death, they did nothing terrible. But since men who had no such power in their whole lives came to write them down, it is one of two things: either they write about what they do not know, without having tried it themselves, or, if they did try, they are the most impious of all men, having given deadly drugs, for the sake of a trial, to people who had done no wrong, and sometimes even to fine and good men. Someone, for instance, seeing two physicians standing by the stalls of the dealers in small wares, brought them honey, supposedly to sell it. They tasted it and haggled over the price, and when they offered him little, he hurried away; and neither of the physicians survived. In all such cases, then, it is right to hate those who wrote them down no less than those who committed them, but even more, inasmuch as it is a lesser wrong to do some evil alone than [to do it] with many. And with the one who committed it, his experience of the evil lore died too; but that of all who wrote it down is immortal, furnishing the wicked with weapons for their crimes. Let us, then, now speak about the things that are useful to human beings, of which we have experience.

[16. On saliva.] Saliva: whether one wishes to call it *sielon*, *sialon* or *ptyelon* makes no difference to me. But one must recognise that its power differs both among the kinds of animals and, within each of them, according to whether the animal is healthy or sick, has eaten or drunk, or is without drink and fasting. For as with urine, bile and sweat, so too the saliva of those who have eaten is weak, while that of people who have gone very thirsty and very hungry is strong and sharp. Midway between the two is that of people who have digested well but have not yet eaten or drunk. It is with this saliva, accordingly, that children's nurses cure lichens, wetting the little finger and then rubbing the affected skin. And they do this often, so that the power from the saliva is preserved in the lichen during the time between applications. Many country people, too, chew wheat grains and put them on boils; for it disperses them and ripens them quickly. Yet if the grains were moistened with water, they do not help in the same way. It is quite clear, then, that the saliva itself supplies the strength of the benefit. On soft bodies and those of children they put chewed bread, not wheat grains. Everything chewed in this way disperses both black eyes and other bruises, and more so when the bread is chewed together with a little radish. In its whole substance saliva is most opposed to the creatures that kill human beings, as Nicander the poet also says somewhere. And a man who promised to show me a spell that kills scorpions said it once and spat on the scorpion, then next said it a second time and spat again, and when he had said it a third time and spat down on it, the scorpion died. Later I myself saw, without the spell, a scorpion die from saliva alone, and suffer this very thing quickly from the saliva of the hungry and thirsty, slowly from that of people filled with food and drink, and proportionately from that of others.

[21. On wolf dung.] A certain man used to give wolves' [dung] to colic sufferers to drink, not only during the attacks but also in the intervals, at least to those who suffered without inflammation. I saw some of them no longer caught by the condition, and those who were caught never again suffering severely, nor even [being caught again] after a short time. That man too preferred to take the whiter dung of wolves, which they excrete when they have eaten bones. I was amazed at it, because even when hung on as an amulet it often clearly helped. This man, then, took dung that had not even fallen to the ground; and this is not hard to do. For that animal is by nature disposed, like the dog, to lift one of its hind legs and urinate and defecate against something that sticks up from the ground. So in the summer season wolf dung is often found on thorn-bushes, and on certain shrubs and fences and on lush herbs. In their dung there is also found some part of the very bones of the animal devoured, which has escaped digestion just as it escaped chewing; this too he used to pound and grind fine and give to colic sufferers to drink. And if the person was fastidious, he mixed in salt and pepper or something of that kind. He gave it for the most part in a wine thin in consistency, but sometimes also in water. As for the dung hung on the patient's flanks, he directed that it should have a fastening, preferably made of wool, and not from any chance sheep; for wool from one torn apart by the wolf would be far better suited to such a use. If such wool was not at hand, he directed that the strap wound around the flanks, and the very thing that would hold the dung, should be of deerskin. We, for our part, put some of the dung into a little pot as big as the largest bean and hung it on some people for the sake of a test, and were amazed to see most of them plainly helped. We made two things like ears on the little pot, through which the strap was passed. This, then, is by the way, if anyone means to trust things hung on in this way: I mean in such a way that what is hung on is a substance, not foreign names, as some of the sorcerers are accustomed [to do]; since I have also tested other substances that act similarly in other conditions. But now is not the time to speak about them; let us go back, then, to the matter in hand.
